candidates.attacker_control: The complete XML document passed to any SAXBuilder build method (InputStream, Reader, File, URL, or InputSource) is attacker-controlled in a typical 'parse untrusted XML' deployment: the attacker supplies the DOCTYPE and <!ENTITY name SYSTEM "..."> declarations, choosing file:// paths (local file disclosure) or http(s):// URLs (SSRF) and arbitrary entity-expansion payloads.
candidates.counterevidence_checked: JDOM provides opt-in mitigations (`setExpandEntities(false)`, `setFeature(SAX_FEATURE_EXTERNAL_ENT,false)`, custom EntityResolver/XMLReaderJDOMFactory), so affectedness depends on application configuration; the weakness is the insecure default. Searches for FEATURE_SECURE_PROCESSING, disallow-doctype-decl, ACCESS_EXTERNAL_DTD, setExpandEntityReferences, and blocking EntityResolver implementations found none in core. JDK/JAXP versions or system properties (e.g. javax.xml.accessExternalDTD) may restrict external access in some deployments, but this code neither sets nor relies on such restrictions. The commented-out advice at SAXBuilder.java:989-990 confirms a blocking resolver was considered and not implemented. The StAX output-side reader (AbstractStAXStreamReader.java:796-803) does disable external entities, showing the project knows the pattern, but that code governs JDOM->StAX output, not SAXBuilder parsing.
candidates.impact: Information disclosure of files readable by the JVM (external entity content is materialized into the parsed JDOM document, which applications commonly log, transform, or echo back), server-side request forgery/outbound network requests to attacker-chosen URLs (external general/parameter entities and external DTDs), and denial of service through large or recursive entity expansion or a blocking network fetch. Applications that parse untrusted XML with default settings are exposed without any obvious API misuse.
candidates.prerequisites: An application uses a default-configured SAXBuilder (or another JDOM reader factory/configuration that leaves external entities enabled and does not install a restricting EntityResolver), and the underlying JAXP/SAX parser resolves external entities by default (typical when no FEATURE_SECURE_PROCESSING / accessExternalDTD restriction is configured). Hardening APIs exist (setExpandEntities(false), setFeature, setEntityResolver, custom XMLReaderJDOMFactory) but are opt-in; safe behavior is not the default.
candidates.root_cause: JDOM's default parse pipeline is built on XMLReaders.NONVALIDATING, which constructs a JAXP SAXParserFactory with only namespaceAware=true and validating=false and never enables any external-entity protection (no XMLConstants.FEATURE_SECURE_PROCESSING, no disallow-doctype-decl, no ACCESS_EXTERNAL_DTD/ACCESS_EXTERNAL_SCHEMA restriction, and no default EntityResolver). SAXBuilder.configureParser then actively sets http://xml.org/sax/features/external-general-entities to the value of its `expand` flag, which defaults to true, and never disables external parameter entities or external DTD loading (load-external-dtd). Consequently, DOCTYPE/entity declarations in attacker-supplied XML are resolved by the underlying parser by default, and the resolved content (e.g. file content) is stored in the resulting JDOM Document; the code comment at SAXBuilder.java:989-990 explicitly notes a blocking EntityResolver is not installed.
candidates.title: Default SAXBuilder/XMLReaders configuration resolves external XML entities (XXE)
candidates.trace: 1) `new SAXBuilder()` selects XMLReaders.NONVALIDATING (SAXBuilder.java:220-222 and 336-347). 2) XMLReaders.NONSingleton builds a SAXParserFactory with only setNamespaceAware(true)/setValidating(false), without any security feature (XMLReaders.java:108-114). 3) build() -> buildEngine() -> configureParser(): `expand` defaults true (SAXBuilder.java:196, setter at 719-722), so the code reads/writes `http://xml.org/sax/features/external-general-entities` with value true (SAXBuilder.java:991-995); external parameter entities and external DTD loading are never disabled. 4) The parser resolves the attacker's external entity, and SAXHandler, whose `expand` is true, does not suppress entity events (SAXHandler.java:925-931), so the resolved characters are flushed into the JDOM tree as normal content that is returned to the caller. No runtime execution was performed; this chain is source-level reasoning.
candidates.unverified: No code was compiled or executed and no exploit payload was run, so runtime exploitability is not confirmed; it depends on the JDK/JAXP parser defaults in the deployment. Whether the benchmark's intended ground-truth issue is exactly this one cannot be checked from the source snapshot. Related but weaker external-access paths (XSLTransformer, caller-supplied StAX XMLInputFactory) were not exhaustively traced. The P1 index explicitly has no control-flow/data-flow or semantic resolution and leaves 4,371 calls unresolved, so index edges were used only for navigation and every claim above is based on source text.
candidates.weakness_type: CWE-611 Improper Restriction of XML External Entity Reference (XXE); insecure default configuration

coverage_summary: Source scope: 261 files (214 Java, ~2.67 MB) with no binary/symlink/sensitive-path exclusions reported. P1 relation index: complete, 3,741 symbols, 9,620 edges, 7,838 calls (4,371 unresolved), 206 navigation facts; the index explicitly implements no data flow or control flow and no semantic resolution, so it was used only for navigation and all findings were verified against source text. Substantively reviewed the default parse path (SAXBuilder, XMLReaders, XMLReaderJAXPFactory, XMLReaderSAX2Factory, XMLReaderXSDFactory/AbstractReaderXSDFactory, SAXHandler, TextBuffer, DTDParser, DOMBuilder, StAX input builders), the output path (Format, AbstractXMLOutputProcessor and related support classes, XMLOutputter), the transform bridge (XSLTransformer, JDOMSource/JDOMResult spot checks), core model validation (Verifier, Attribute, Element, Text, CDATA, Comment, ProcessingInstruction, Namespace, EntityRef, DocType spot checks), and internals (ArrayCopy, StringBin, ReflectionConstructor, SystemProperty, JDOMConstants). Repository-wide literal searches were run for process execution, network connections, file writes, Class.forName, System.getProperty, ObjectInputStream, secure-processing/external-access constants, disallow-doctype-decl, load-external-dtd, and EntityResolver implementations. Not exhaustively reviewed line-by-line: most of contrib, core/samples, the XPath/Jaxen subsystem, and large parts of Element/ContentList internals.
limitations: No execution, compilation, unit tests, scanners, or exploit payloads were run; all conclusions are static source-text inferences and no finding is runtime-confirmed.
The single candidate is capped by instruction; other plausible-but-weaker leads are listed as rejected/unconfirmed rather than additional candidates.

Exploitability of the XXE default depends on the deployment's JDK/JAXP parser defaults and on whether the host application already applies hardening (custom XMLReaderJDOMFactory, EntityResolver, setExpandEntities(false), accessExternalDTD/FEATURE_SECURE_PROCESSING system configuration).
The P1 index has no control-flow/data-flow or semantic resolution and 4,371 unresolved calls; absence of an index edge (e.g. a Verifier call) is not evidence of absence in source.
The build.xml references a ./test tree and maven/jars that are absent from the snapshot, so test-based evidence of intended behavior could not be consulted.
Contrib modules and samples (not part of the published jdom2 core artifact) received only targeted spot checks.

rejected_leads.lead: XSLTransformer uses the default TransformerFactory with no FEATURE_SECURE_PROCESSING / ACCESS_EXTERNAL_STYLESHEET / ACCESS_EXTERNAL_DTD restriction (core/src/java/org/jdom2/transform/XSLTransformer.java:125-133, 244-255).
rejected_leads.reason: A real external-access configuration gap, but it requires attacker-controlled XSLT stylesheets plus XSLT-engine behavior, is caller-dependent, and is a weaker, less direct data path than the default SAXBuilder parsing path.

rejected_leads.lead: Reflective class loading driven by system properties in XPath/XPathFactory and contrib XPathMatcher (core/src/java/org/jdom2/xpath/XPath.java:126-141, core/src/java/org/jdom2/xpath/XPathFactory.java:102-103, contrib/src/java/org/jdom2/contrib/input/scanner/XPathMatcher.java:373-384).
rejected_leads.reason: Requires control over JVM system properties (local/admin capability), not attacker-supplied XML, so it does not represent an external attacker-controlled input path; also constrained by assignability checks (ReflectionConstructor.java:79-87).

rejected_leads.lead: Regex-based DTD parsing in core/src/java/org/jdom2/input/stax/DTDParser.java (pattern built at lines 190-221).
rejected_leads.reason: A crafted DTD string could cause backtracking in `(.*)\](\s*)>`-style matching, but the input is bounded to DTD text supplied by an already-configured StAX reader and no exponential/catastrophic behavior was demonstrated from source; unconfirmed.

rejected_leads.lead: Java serialization entry points in Document.java:909-920, Element.java:2077-2099 and JDOMCoreNavigator.java:328-332.
rejected_leads.reason: readObject methods only re-establish internal state and call JDOM setters; no gadget chain or dangerous deserialization sink exists inside JDOM itself, and exploitation would require the host application to deserialize untrusted data. Unconfirmed.
Attribute values are double-quoted and `&`, `<`, `>`, `"`, CR, NL and TAB are escaped, CDATA rejects `]]>`, comments reject `--`, and PI data rejects `?>`; no escaping defect found.

rejected_leads.lead: Contrib BeanMapper/XML->bean reflection and JDOMBean file access.
rejected_leads.reason: These are demonstration/contrib utilities outside the published core artifact; the class-name derivation is driven by the mapping configuration rather than by attacker XML alone, and no concrete attacker-controlled sink was traced.

summary: Reviewed the 261-file JDOM 2.x snapshot (214 Java files) as a defensive source review. The strongest source-evidenced issue is in the default XML parsing pipeline: `SAXBuilder` defaults to `XMLReaders.NONVALIDATING`, which creates a JAXP `SAXParserFactory` with no XXE mitigation (no `FEATURE_SECURE_PROCESSING`, no `disallow-doctype-decl`, no `ACCESS_EXTERNAL_DTD`/schema restriction, no default `EntityResolver`), and `SAXBuilder.configureParser` explicitly sets `http://xml.org/sax/features/external-general-entities` to the `expand` value, which defaults to `true`. A malicious XML document's DOCTYPE/external entity declarations are therefore resolved by the underlying parser and the fetched content is placed into the parsed JDOM tree, giving file disclosure, SSRF, and denial-of-service exposure to any application that parses untrusted XML with default settings. This matches the known JDOM XXE weakness class (CVE-2021-33813) and no counter-vailing protection exists anywhere in the snapshot (searches for secure-processing/external-access constants and blocking resolvers returned nothing). Other leads (XSLTransformer factory defaults, system-property reflective loading, DTDParser regex parsing, Java deserialization, output escaping) were examined and were weaker or showed no defect.
